passage: At 3 a.m. in her Pune flat, Chandrika walked the hallway with her crying baby and thought of her own father, Amandeep, who had done this with three children and a long bus commute. She remembered him falling asleep over his tea, and her fury when he missed her school recital. Now the fury had a crack in it. In the morning Amandeep arrived with a steel tiffin of poha. "You look tired, beta," he said. She nearly cried. "Papa, how did you manage us?" He laughed. "Badly, some days." She said quietly, "I'm going to be home for my child's recitals, Papa, even if I have to move a meeting." He nodded, said nothing, and pressed the tiffin into her hands. Her respect for him had grown. So had the ache.

qa.q: What did Amandeep bring in the morning?
qa.a: Amandeep arrived with a steel tiffin of poha.

qa.q: What is Chandrika feeling toward her father as she walks the hallway at 3 a.m.?
qa.a: New tenderness mixed with old hurt: the fury 'had a crack in it', and she nearly cried when he called her tired.

qa.q: What does Chandrika decide to do differently from her father?
qa.a: She resolves to be home for her child's recitals, even if she has to move a meeting.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt hearing Chandrika ask how he managed?
qa.a: Amandeep may have felt seen but a little exposed; he laughed and admitted 'Badly, some days,' then pressed the tiffin into her hands without a word.

grounding: A new parent starts to see how hard her own parents had it, feels tenderness and leftover anger, and still names what she will do differently.

passage:
I'm Pema, and my son is ten months old. Last week, at three in the morning, rocking him in the dark, I suddenly thought of my mother.

Urmila, my Amala, raised me alone in Kalimpong. She sold momos from a cart all evening and came home after I was asleep. As a child I hated that cart. I remember eating cold rice alone and crying for her, and some of that anger is still in me.

But now I'm a mother too, with a husband, a washing machine and a salary, and I'm still exhausted. How did she do it with nothing? I cried, rocking my son, for the girl I was and for the woman she was.

I called her in the morning and just said, "Amala, thank you. I didn't know." She laughed and said, "Now you know."

I'm still going to do some things differently. I won't leave my son to eat alone. But I understand her now.

qa.q: What did Pema's mother sell from a cart?
qa.a: She sold momos from a cart all evening.

qa.q: What did Pema feel, rocking the baby at three in the morning?
qa.a: Pema felt a new tenderness for her mother, mixed with old anger and sadness for the lonely child she had been.

qa.q: How does Pema hold both respect and change?
qa.a: She thanks her mother and understands her struggle, while still naming that she won't leave her son to eat alone.

qa.q: How might Urmila have felt hearing her daughter's thanks?
qa.a: Urmila probably felt moved and quietly vindicated, laughing and saying, "Now you know."

grounding: A first-person account shows a new mother who now sees how hard her own mother had it, feeling tenderness and some anger, deepening respect while naming what she will do differently.

passage:
Fathers' group note, session five, community centre, Pune.

Abhinav, 26, spoke for the first time today. His daughter is four months old. He said that walking her at night, he has started thinking about his own father, who drove a tempo sixteen hours a day and came home short-tempered. "I used to hate him for shouting. Now I'm this tired after one baby, and he had four of us."

His voice broke. He said he feels tenderness for his father for the first time and, in the same breath, still angry about the shouting.

Asif, another father, said, "You can understand him and still not become him." Abhinav nodded hard.

I asked him to write two lists: what he now respects in his father, and what he will do differently. He wrote four things on the first list. On the second, one line: "I will not shout at my children to let out my tiredness." He plans to call his father this weekend.

qa.q: How many hours a day did Abhinav's father drive the tempo?
qa.a: He drove a tempo sixteen hours a day.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Abhinav describe about his father?
qa.a: Abhinav felt tenderness for his father for the first time, alongside lingering anger about the shouting.

qa.q: How did the group leader help Abhinav use this new understanding?
qa.a: By asking him to write what he respects in his father and what he will do differently, so respect grows without excusing the shouting.

qa.q: What did Asif offer from his own view as a father?
qa.a: Asif offered the idea that Abhinav can understand his father and still choose not to become him.

grounding: A group leader's note shows a new father who begins to see how hard his own father had it, feeling tenderness and anger, deepening respect while naming what he will do differently.
